Citation:

Dhami et al v.
CBC et al

Date:

20011228

2001 BCSC 1811

Docket:

S045565

Registry:
New Westminster

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

BETWEEN:

MANJIT SINGH DHAMI, HARJIT SINGH
ATWAL,

PIARA SINGH NATT and JAGTAR SINGH
SANDHU

plaintiffs

AND:

canadian broadcasting
corporation,

kevin evans, indo-canadian times
international inc.,

indo-canadian times, tara singh
hayer,

dalip singh mangat, sohinder
singh dhillon and

harjinder singh dhillon

Defendants

RULING

OF THE

HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE
SLADE

Counsel for the Plaintiffs:

Eric
Rice Q.C.

Counsel for the Defendants CBC

And Kevin Evans:

Murray
Smith

Date and Place of Hearing:

June
7 and 8, 2001

New
Westminster, BC

I.   Overview of Facts

[
1
]

The Statement of Claim was filed on May 26,
1999.  The Statement of Defence was filed on November 1, 1999, and an amended
Statement of Defence was filed on August 15, 2000.  The matter has been set for
trial before a jury in February 2003.

[
2
]

The plaintiffs were members of the executive of
the Guru Nanak Sikh Temple, located in Surrey, B.C., at various times between
1986 and 1997.  The defendant Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (“CBC”) is a
national broadcasting corporation.  The defendant Kevin Evans was, at the time
of the alleged defamatory broadcast, the chief journalist for television news
and current affairs, CBC, British Columbia.  The defendant Indo-Canadian Times
International Inc. was the publisher of the newspaper Indo-Canadian Times, a
Punjabi language newspaper published weekly with a circulation in the Sikh
community of British Columbia.  The remaining individually named defendants
were members of the so-called “moderate” faction in the Temple.

[
3
]

On March 7, 1997, CBC broadcast a television
program in British Columbia in which the individually named defendants made
statements that are alleged by the plaintiffs to be defamatory.  This program
was re-broadcast in whole or in part on the CBC’s national broadcast service,
and the program was re-broadcast again in British Columbia on March 11, 1997.

[
4
]

This Ruling is concerned with certain
applications that have been brought as between the plaintiffs and the
defendants, CBC and Kevin Evans.

[
5
]

The words complained of by the plaintiffs are
set out in Schedule “A” to the Statement of Claim, and are reproduced below:

Kevin Evans: - “Why did the ISYF want control
of the Surrey Temple in the mid eighties.  The Federation claims one reason is
because the Temple provided a political platform.”

Kevin Evans: - “Others claim that’s a
smokescreen for the real purpose of the ISYF.”

Harjinder Dhillon: - “If they hold the Temple
then they collect the money and they can spend wherever they want.”

Kevin Evans: - “Few in the lower mainland Sikh
community believe the talk that the ISYF was funnelling money to Sikh militants
in India.  Members of the current Temple executive believe the ISYF has a more
basic motivation in wanting to control the Temple.”

Dalip Mangat: - “Because they have a common
interest.  The common purpose is just to keep control of the Gurdwara.”

Kevin Evans: - “For what purpose.”

Dalip Mangat: - “Purpose for that which I told
you - for power and money to use it.”

Kevin Evans: - “And they’re using the power and
the money for what?”

Dalip Mangat: - “Using the power for their
self-interest and the money - it’s not clear unless I see the records where
they use the money.  But people have suspicions the money has not been spent
legitimately.”

Kevin Evans: - “The suspicion persists because
the old ISYF executive has refused to hand over the financial books for the
years 1985 to 1993.  And because some of those involved in those years suddenly
came into money.”

Sohinder Dhillon: - “There are some people who
are rich - quite rich these days.  And they have been on the Gurdwara (Temple
executive).  This is what I can say.”

Kevin Evans: - “Piara Natt was a truck driver
during his early days with the ISYF and the Surrey Temple.  In 1993, he
purchased land in Surrey where he built this home.  He also bought a nearby
rental property and also that year formed Natt Trucking after buying several
new trucks.  Mr. Natt did not reply to our request for an interview.

Harjit Atwal was in the stucco business.  In
recent years, he’s partnered with several other ISYF members to form companies
that have developed real estate.  Like Cougar Creek development which paid
575,000 in 1991 for the land in which they built this condo complex.  Like
Cardinal’s Court Development.  The land alone for this project cost 3/4 of a
million in 1993.  The same year Atwal’s Fraserview Terrace Limited bought this
land for nearly a half million.  Trying to get rezoning for a hotel.  Harjit
Atwal refused to be interviewed on camera for this report.  But he did have
this to say on the phone:”

Kevin Evans: - “Manjit Dhami works the night
shift at a sawmill.  He lives in this home he built last year.  The same year
he developed two houses and three lots in Langley.”

Kevin Evans: “The current acting Temple
president says if there is nothing to hide then the old executive should just
hand over the records.”

Balwant Singh Gill: - “It should be an
independent audit.  And the only way you can audit is if you have the records
of the Temple.  Records should be in the Temple.”

Kevin Evans: - “Will the financial records ever
be handed over?  Will the struggle which has been over much more than tables
and chairs continue?  Who knows?  But there is change in the air.  A new group
has been formed called Sikhs against terrorism and it’s hoping people will
accept invitation to come to this community hall on Sunday afternoon for a
public meeting to speak out about what has really happened at the Sikh Temple
over the last 10 years.  A small group had tarnished the image of the entire
community.  For Broadcast 1, I am Kevin Evans.”

[
6
]

The Amended Statement of Claim of the defendants
CBC and Kevin Evans denies that the program was defamatory, and also pleads
qualified privilege, justification, fair comment, and that the impugned
broadcast is privileged and protected under
s. 2(b)
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.

II.  Applications

[
7
]

The following applications were brought:

(a)
Application by the defendants to strike the Statement of Claim as disclosing no
reasonable cause of action.

(b)
Application by the plaintiffs to strike the defendants plea of justification as
disclosing no reasonable defence.

(c)
Application by the plaintiffs to strike the plea of qualified privilege as
disclosing no reasonable defence.

(d)
Application by the plaintiffs to strike the
Charter
defence as
disclosing no reasonable defence.

(e)  Application
by the defendants for particulars:

1)   of the
facts on which the plaintiffs rely in support of their complaint that the words
were used in a derogatory sense, and

2)   particulars
identifying the photographic images on which the plaintiffs rely in support of
their claim of defamatory meaning, and

3)   particulars
of various allegations set out under the plaintiffs general allegation of
malice, and

4)   particulars
of the plaintiffs’ claim of loss of income, damage to reputation, and special
damages.

(f)  Application
by the plaintiffs to strike particulars delivered by the defendants relating to
qualified privilege, justification, and fair comment.

(g)  Application
by the defendants for disclosure of plaintiffs financial documents.

III. Discussion and Rulings on
Applications

A.   Defendants’ Application to
strike Statement of Claim

[
8
]

The essence of the plaintiffs’ claim of
defamation is that the publication by the defendants of statements alleging a
failure on the part of named members of the former executive of the Surrey Sikh
Temple to provide an accounting for donations to the temple, and their having
become personally wealthy during their tenure, constitute defamation.  The
force of the allegations, and their tenor, is said to be amplified by the tone
of voice and facial expressions of the defendant Kevin Evans in a broadcast
published and republished by the defendant CBC.  The plaintiffs say in
paragraph 15 of the Statement of Claim that these statements “were defamatory
in that they meant and were understood to mean that the plaintiffs had engaged
in criminal conduct, namely the misappropriation of funds from the Temple, and
that therefore they were dishonest and corrupt”.

[
9
]

The defendants demanded particulars “of the
facts and matters on which the plaintiffs rely in support of the complaint that
the words were used in a derogatory sense other than their ordinary meaning”.

[
10
]

The plaintiffs’ response was that “the plaintiffs say that the words
complained of were derogatory according to their ordinary meaning”.

[
11
]

The defendants argue that the plaintiffs rely on innuendo, and place
reliance on Rule 19(12)(a), which provides:

(12) In an action for libel or slander,

(a)  where the plaintiff alleges that the words or matter complained of were
used in a derogatory sense other than their ordinary meaning, the plaintiff
shall give particulars of the facts and matters on which the plaintiff relies
in support of that sense, …

and say that in the absence of a
responsive demand for particulars, the Statement of Claim should be struck under
Rule 19(24) as disclosing no reasonable claim.

[
12
]

The power to strike out a pleading on the ground that it discloses
no reasonable cause of action should be exercised only where the case is
absolutely beyond doubt:
McNaughton

v.

Baker

(1988),
1988 CanLII 3036 (BC CA)
, 25 B.C.L.R. (2d) 17 (C.A.).  In a defamation action, where the
pleadings are of particular importance, the court may grant leave to amend the
pleadings rather than striking out the action.  See:
Lapointe
v.

Summach
,
[1999] B.C.J. No. 1459 (Q.L.)(B.C.S.C.)(Master)
.

[
13
]

The following issues arise:

(i)  Is the plaintiffs’ Statement of Claim based on innuendo?

(ii) If yes, should particulars be ordered pursuant to Rule
19(12)(a)?

(iii)If no,
should particulars nevertheless be ordered

pursuant to Rule 19(16), to specify all possible

meanings that could arise out of the words

published?

1.  Is the Plaintiffs’ Statement of
Claim based on

innuendo?

[
14
]

The defendants argue that the broadcast used no words which could be
construed as meaning misappropriation of funds or dishonesty or corruption.
They state, further, that unless actual words with that meaning were used, the
plaintiffs are required to plead and particularize the innuendo.

[
15
]

It is necessary to consider, first, whether the plaintiffs have pled
an inference beyond the ‘natural and ordinary’ meaning of the words (otherwise
termed a ‘false innuendo’) or a ‘true or legal innuendo’.  The distinction
between the two is important.  A ‘true or legal innuendo’ gives rise to a
separate cause of action under the law of defamation.  A plea of a ‘true
innuendo’ must be particularized pursuant to Rule 19(12)(a).

[
16
]

A.M. Linden, in
Canadian Tort Law
, 5
th
ed.
(Toronto: Butterworths, 1993) summarizes the law of innuendo as follows at p.
644:

Words, which appear innocent on the surface,
may be defamatory to certain people who are aware of other facts, not generally
known, in relation to thereto.  The law of defamation recognizes two different
situations in this regard:  (1) words which have a technical or slang meaning
or a meaning which depends on some special knowledge possessed by a limited
number of persons only, and (2) ordinary words which may on occasion bear some
special meaning other that their natural and ordinary meaning because of some
extrinsic facts or circumstances.

These “special meanings” are described as
“legal” or “true” innuendos, as distinguishable from the vernacular usage of
the term as encompassing reasonable inferences, which one may draw from the
ordinary and natural meaning of the words
.  The plaintiff
must plead a legal innuendo and must prove the underlying facts or
circumstances.  (Emphasis added.)

[
17
]

In
Lewis

v.

Daily Telegraph, Ltd
.,

[1963] 2 All E.R. 151 (H.L.)
, two newspapers published statements that officers
of the City of London Fraud Squad were inquiring into the affairs of the
plaintiff’s company.  The plaintiff pled that the statements meant that he had
been guilty of fraud or was suspected of fraud.  The House of Lords considered
whether, where a plaintiff puts forward an extended ordinary meaning, the
defendant is entitled to a ruling as to whether the words were capable of
bearing that particular meaning.  The majority of the court held that the
defendant was entitled to such a ruling before the statements are left to the
jury.  In its analysis the court found the ordinary man would not infer guilt
of fraud merely from the existence of an inquiry.  The jury should have been
instructed as such. They were not; therefore, a new trial was ordered.  The
court examined the phrase ‘natural and ordinary’ meaning as well as the
pleading requirements for true and false innuendoes.

[
18
]

With respect to ‘natural and ordinary’ meaning, Lord Reid, writing
for the majority, summarized the law as follows:

What the ordinary man would infer without
special knowledge has generally been called the natural and ordinary meaning of
the words.  But that expression is rather misleading in that it conceals the
fact that there are two elements in it.  Sometimes it is not necessary to go
beyond the words themselves as where the plaintiff has been called a thief or a
murderer.
But more often the sting is not so much in the words themselves
as in what the ordinary man will infer from them and that is also regarded as
part of their natural and ordinary meaning
.  (at p. 154)  (Emphasis added.)

[
19
]

At p. 166, Lord Hodson stated that inferential meanings arising from
‘natural and ordinary’ words are commonly referred to as ‘false innuendoes’.
There is no separate cause of action for false innuendoes.

[
20
]

Lord Morris of Borth-Y-Gest, dissented on the issue of whether the
words were capable in their ‘natural and ordinary’ meaning of an inference of
guilt of fraud.  He concurred in the result, and commented generally on
pleadings in defamation.  At p. 160, his Lordship stated:

[A plaintiff] may establish that because there
were extrinsic facts which were known to readers of the words, such readers
would be reasonably induced to understand the words in a defamatory sense which
went beyond or which altered their natural and ordinary meaning and which could
be regarded as a secondary or as an extended meaning.  …
A defamatory meaning
which derives no support from extrinsic facts, but which is said to be implied
from the words which are used, is not a true innuendo….

…Though the two paragraphs [of the statement of
claim] were undoubtedly pleaded as innuendoes, once it was clear that the
contention of the plaintiffs was that the words themselves would be understood
by ordinary readers to be conveying and expressing the meanings recorded in those
paragraphs, then the case for the plaintiffs was direct and straightforward…

[
21
]

Lord Delvin held that the plaintiff’s Statement of Claim should
include three separate paragraphs:

In the first paragraph the defamatory words
will be set out as hitherto.  It may be that they will speak for themselves.
If not, a second paragraph will set out those innuendoes or indirect meanings
that go beyond the literal meaning of the words but which the pleader claims to
be inherent in them.  Thirdly, if the pleader has the necessary material, he
can plead a secondary meaning or legal innuendo supported by particulars….  (p.
171)

[
22
]

Lord Delvin noted that the important distinction between the second
paragraph and the third is the requirement of particulars only with respect to
the third.  As an alternative he also stated that the pleader can “plead in the
second paragraph that the words in their natural and ordinary meaning were
understood to mean one thing; and then he could plead in the third paragraph
that, by reason of the facts thereinafter, they were understood to mean
another”.

[
23
]

In the present case the plaintiffs have followed Lord Delvin’s
guidance with respect to the first and second paragraphs.  They say that there
is no plea of secondary meaning or legal innuendo, that they have not plead
innuendo, and that particulars are therefore not required.

[
24
]

Lord Delvin’s guidelines have not been applied in Canada.  However,
in
Fletcher-Gordon et al
. v
. Southam Inc
.,
[1995] B.C.J.
No. 253 (Q.L.)(B.C.S.C.)(Master)
, aff’d,
[1995] B.C.J. No. 879 (Q.L.)(B.C.S.C)
,
the court considered the following paragraph in a pleading:  “In their natural
and ordinary meaning the impugned words in the previous paragraphs meant and
were understood to mean….”  The court held the pleading to be unnecessary, but
not improper.  The court went on to order particulars requiring the plaintiffs
to set out the portions of the article to be defamatory.  The plaintiffs in the
present case have, in Schedule “A” to their Statement of Claim, set out the
portions of the broadcast they claim to be defamatory.

[
25
]

The principle as stated in
Lewis
, that ‘natural and
ordinary’ meaning includes the inferences that an ordinary man would draw from
the words has been cited with approval in Canadian courts.  See:
Ward

v.

Clark
(2000), 77 B.C.L.R. (3d) 364,
2000 BCSC
979
at para.
40
, rev’d on other grounds [2001] B.C.J. No. 2687,
2001 BCCA 724
;
Taylor-Wright

v
.

CHBC-TV
,
a division of WIC Television
,

[1999] B.C.J. No. 334 (Q.L.)(B.C.S.C.) at para. 24
;
Leenan

v
.

Canadian Broadcasting Corp.
(2001), 54 O.R. (3d) 612 (Ont. C.A.),
at para. 8
;
Ross

v
.
New Brunswick Teachers’
Assn
. (2001),
2001 NBCA 62 (CanLII)
, 201 D.L.R. (4th) 75 (N.B.C.A.) at para.
25
.  These cases
adopt the law on this point from
Lewis
, but do not provide any
further analysis.

[
26
]

It is clear that the common law definition of ‘natural and ordinary’
meaning includes inferences which an ordinary man would draw.  The plaintiffs
do not allege that the words are defamatory only by reason of extrinsic
circumstances.  As such, ‘true innuendo’ has not been pled.  The plaintiffs
allege that the words were “defamatory in that they meant and were understood
to mean that the plaintiffs had engaged in criminal conduct, namely the
misappropriation of funds from the Temple, and that therefore they were dishonest
and corrupt”.

[
27
]

The Statement of Claim does not use the words “ordinary meaning”.
The allegation of “ordinary meaning” is set out in the particulars provided by
the plaintiffs in response to the defendants’ demand.  This demand was made
after the Statement of Defence was filed.

[
28
]

On a reading of para. 15, it is clear that the plaintiffs allege
defamation and, in support of this claim, they set out what the words were
meant and understood to mean.  They have in essence pled a ‘false innuendo’ in
para. 15 without including the words ‘natural and ordinary’ meaning.  Those
words appear in their answer to the defendants’ Demand for Particulars.

[
29
]

The claim of defamation, based as it is on the words spoken and a
statement of the inference that is said to arise, is sufficient to disclose a
reasonable cause of action.  That claim permits a determination of whether the
words are, in their ordinary meaning, capable of a defamatory meaning.  That
determination will be made by the trial judge at the appropriate time.  Should
the trial judge so find, it will be for the jury to determine whether the
defendants have in fact been defamed.

2.   Are
the plaintiffs required to provide further

particulars pursuant to Rule 19(12)(a)?

[
30
]

Rule 19(12)(a) of the
Rules of Court
, provides that,
in an action for libel or slander,

(a)  where the plaintiff
alleges that the
words or matter complained of were used in a derogatory sense other that their
ordinary meaning
, the plaintiff shall give particulars of the facts and
matters on which the plaintiff relies in support of that sense…

[
31
]

The plaintiff relies on the ordinary meaning of the words spoken.
This is a plea that relies on false innuendo, not true innuendo.  Rule
19(12)(a) has no application.

3.

Should particulars be ordered pursuant to

Rule 19(16)?

[
32
]

My ruling under heading (ii), above, does not fully answer the
question whether particulars of defamatory meaning should be ordered.  The
defendants could be taken by surprise if, at trial, the plaintiffs based their
claim on a particular portion of the broadcast, or a different defamatory
meaning from that specifically pled.  In the absence of a plea of legal or true
innuendo, an order for particulars could be made under Rule 19(16):

Rule 19(16):

The court may order a party to deliver further
and better particulars of a matter stated in a pleading.

[
33
]

Courts have generally considered Rule 19(16) with respect to
requests for further and better particulars where the plaintiff has pled an
entire article, letter or broadcast but failed to specify the matter or words
alleged to be defamatory.  See:
Bank of B.C.

v.

CBC

(1986),
1986 CanLII 937 (BC SC)
, 5 B.C.L.R. (2d) 131 (B.C.S.C.), leave to appeal refused (1986),

1986 CanLII 984 (BC CA)
, 6 B.C.L.R. (2d) 215 (C.A.);
Moffat

v
. BCTV Systems Ltd.
1984 CanLII 507 (BC SC)
, [1985]
1 WWR 271 (B.C.S.C.) and
Fletcher-Gordon et al
. v
. Southam Inc
.,

[1995] B.C.J. No. 253 (Q.L.)(B.C.S.C.)(Master)
, aff’d ,
[1995] B.C.J. No. 879
(Q.L.)(B.C.S.C)
.

[
34
]

In
The Law of Defamation in Canada
, 2
nd
ed.
(Toronto: Carswell, 1994) at p. 1308, R.E. Brown summarizes the law as follows:

Where the words are alleged to be defamatory in
their ordinary sense, the court may order particulars of the sense in which the
plaintiff claims the words reasonably could be understood, if the words are
such that
more than one meaning is possible
and the meaning is not
otherwise abundantly clear….

[
35
]

The plaintiffs rely on
Bank of B.C.

v.

CBC
,
as authority for the proposition that particulars are generally not required
where the message is fairly short and simple.  This decision does not, however,
foreclose a valid demand for particulars where more than one defamatory meaning
can be gleaned from a short article.

4.   Must the
Statement of Claim be further

particularized?

[
36
]

In
Lewis
, Lord Morris of Borth-Y-Gest held that it was
not essential for a plaintiff to set out the meanings that could be inferred
from the words.  At p. 160, he stated:

…In a case where there is no innuendo pleaded,
it is not essential for a plaintiff to record and define in his pleadings what
he says are the ordinary or direct or natural or implied meanings of the
words.
If however, he does do so (as may often be helpful provided it is
made clear what is being done) and, if the judge considers that the words are
capable of bearing any one or more of such meanings, he ought so to rule.  If
the plaintiff does not do so the various meanings suggested by the plaintiff
will almost invariably be canvassed during the trial and if the judge considers
that the words are not capable of bearing any one or more of them again he
ought so to rule
.  (Emphasis added.)

Lord Hodgson
also stated, at pp. 166-67:

A pleader is entitled to allege in his
statement of claim what the words in their natural and ordinary meaning convey,
provided he makes it clear that he is not relying on a true innuendo, which
gives a separate cause of action and requires a separate verdict from the
jury.  It is desirable that he should do so, for, where there is no true
innuendo, the judge should define the limits of the natural and ordinary
meaning of the libel and leave to the jury only those meanings which he rules
are capable of being defamatory.
If the natural and ordinary meaning is
pleaded the defense will know what the contentions of the plaintiff are, and
the judge will not have to analyze the submissions of counsel in his charge to the
jury without having the benefit of a pleading setting out what those
submissions are.
(Emphasis added.)

At pp. 174-75 of the same
case, Lord Delvin stated:

It is undoubtedly the law that the judge should
not leave the question "libel or no libel" to the jury unless the
words are reasonably capable of a defamatory meaning.  But if several
defamatory meanings are pleaded or suggested, can the judge direct the jury
that the words are capable of one meaning but not of another?  The point is
important here, because the defendants admit that the words are defamatory in
one sense but dispute that they are defamatory in the senses pleaded in the
statements of claim, and contend that the judge should have so directed the
jury.  Both counsel for the appellants appear at one time to have argued in the
Court of Appeal that the function of the judge was exhausted when he ruled that
the words were capable of being defamatory; and that it was not for him to
inquire whether they were or were not capable of any particular defamatory
meaning.  But later they abandoned the point; and, therefore, did not initiate
the discussion of it here.  Nevertheless there was considerable discussion of
it, because some of your lordships at one time felt that it was a point which
ought to be considered.
In the result I think that all your lordships are
now clearly of the opinion that the judge must rule whether the words are
capable of bearing each of the defamatory meanings, if there be more than one,
put forward by the plaintiff.  This supports indirectly my view on the
desirability of pleading different meanings
.  If the plaintiff can get
before the jury only those meanings, which the judge rules, as capable of being
defamatory, there is good reason for having the meanings alleged set out
precisely as part of the record.  (Emphasis added.)

[
37
]

In
Stumpf
v.

Globe Holdings Ltd
. (1982),

1982 CanLII 1217 (AB QB)
, 45 A.R. 298 (Alta. Q.B.)(Master), the court adopted
Lewis
on this
point.  In
Stumpf
, the defendant applied for an order requiring
the plaintiff to answer certain questions he refused to answer in discovery.
The court referred with approval to the above passage from
Lewis,
however
the court dismissed the defendant’s application for discovery as to meaning of
the words.  At para. 17, Master Funduck stated that “whether the words, in
their ordinary and natural meaning, are libellous is solely for the trier of
fact to decide.  In such a case a defendant cannot, on examinations for
discovery, ask a plaintiff to point to any particular words as sustaining an
alleged ordinary and natural meaning which is libelous”.  The court held that
merely because the plaintiff chooses to set out meanings does not entitle the
defendant to then require the plaintiff to specify words with particular
meanings.

[
38
]

In
DDSA Pharmaceuticals Ltd
.
v.

Times
Newspapers Ltd. and another
,
[1972] 3 All ER 417 (C.A.)
, the plaintiff
company manufactured drugs and claimed to be able to do so at a lower cost than
international companies.  The first defendant published a lengthy article
written by the second defendant.  The plaintiff alleged that the words in the
article were defamatory.  The plaintiff relied on the article in its entirety
without specifying the defamatory portions.  The defendant had applied to the
master for an order striking out the statement of claim for failing to disclose
a cause of action.  The master made the order.  The order was reversed on
appeal.  On further appeal, the Court of Appeal reinstated the master’s
decision.  The pleadings were struck as embarrassing and defective.  Lord
Denning for the unanimous court, held that the pleading was defective.  At p.
419, he stated:

In the first place, there ought to have been an
innuendo pleaded.  This article is capable of many different meanings – so many
that it was necessary for the fair conduct of the trial that there should be
pleaded a ‘popular’ or ‘false’ innuendo, or whatever you like to call it.  In
that innuendo, the plaintiffs should set out the meaning or meanings, which
they say the words bear.
This is necessary, not only for the fair conduct
of the trial, but also to enable the defendant to know what to plead, whether
to plead justification or fair comment or to apologize.
I need not go
through all the cases.  They are
Allsop
v.
Church of England
Newspapers
,
[1972] 2 All ER 26
;
S and K Holdings Ktd
.
v
.

Throgmorton Publications Ltd
.
,
[1972] 1 WLR 1036
and also
Associated
Leisure Ltd
.
v
.
Associated Newspapers Ltd
.
(1972) The
Times, 24
th
March.  Those cases establish that in most cases, if not
all,
it is necessary for the plaintiffs, even when they rely on the natural

Toronto Sun Publishing
Corp

[1986] 2 All E.R.
84 (C.A.)

Simply put, if the plaintiff is entitled to

[

Lord Nicholls, whose judgment was endorsed by two of the other Law

determine whether an occasion was privileged in cases not fitting within the

Lord Nicholls held, at p. 616:

The requirement that both the maker of the
statement and the recipient must have an interest or duty draws attention to
the need to have regard to the position of both parties when deciding whether
an occasion is privileged.  But this should not be allowed to obscure the
rationale of the underlying public interest on which privilege is founded.  The
essence of this defence lies in the law's recognition of the need, in the
public interest, for a particular recipient to receive frank and uninhibited
communication of particular information from a particular source.  That is the
end the law is concerned to attain.  The protection afforded to the maker of
the statement is the means by which the law seeks to achieve that end.  Thus
the court has to assess whether, in the public interest, the publication should
be protected in the absence of malice.

account include the following.  The comments are illustrative only.

1.

The seriousness of the allegation.  The more serious the charge, the
more the public is misinformed and the individual harmed, if the allegation is
not true.

2.

The nature of the information, and the extent to which the
subject-matter is a matter of public concern.

3.

The source of the information.  Some informants have no direct
knowledge of the events.  Some have their own axes to grind, or are being paid
for their stories.

4.

The steps taken to verify the information.

5.

The status of the information.  The allegation may have already been
the subject of an investigation which commands respect.

6.

The urgency of the matter.  News is often a perishable commodity.

7.

Whether comment was sought from the defendant.  He may have
information others do not possess or have not disclosed.  An approach to the defendant
will not always be necessary.

8.

Whether the article contained the gist of the plaintiff's side of
the story.

9.

The tone of the article.  A newspaper can raise queries or call for
an investigation. It need not adopt allegations as statements of fact.

10.

The circumstances of the publication, including
the timing.

exhaustive.  The weight to be given to these and any other relevant factors

the jury, if there is one.

privilege, His Lordship held, at p. 625-6:

supra

supra

basis of a duty/interest relationship.

[

and to the extent they were comment, the words complained of were fair comment
upon a matter of public interest which were spoken in good faith and with
honest belief.

[
143
]

The plaintiffs’ demand for particulars is as
follows:

2.(a)     As to paragraph 7 of the Statement of
Defence:  Which of the words complained of were statements of fact and which
were statements of comment?

[
144
]

The defendants’ answer is prefaced with the
statement, “The words complained of in the Statement of Claim were statements
of comment except for the following words which were statements of fact”.
Sub-paragraphs (a) to (q) in the answer purport to the particulars of
statements of fact.  In relation to those, I find as follows:

(1)  The
answers in sub-paragraphs (a) and (b) are struck.  A suspicion of a fact is not
a fact.

(2)  Sub-paragraphs
(c) to (i) are not struck, as they are presented as statements of fact.

(3)  Sub-paragraph
(j) is responsive to certain words complained of by the plaintiffs, and, as
such, is a statement of fact.

(4)  Sub-paragraphs
(k) to (p) are not struck, as they are statements of fact.

(5)  Sub-paragraph
(q) is a portion of the broadcast, and is presented in this answer as a
statement of fact.  It is not struck.

(6)  Sub-paragraphs
(r) to (t) relate to portions of the broadcast that pertain to certain of the
plaintiffs employment (r), and their alleged acquisition of property (s, t).
As such, these are statements of fact, and are not struck.

(7)  Sub-paragraph
(u) refers to documents which relate to political issues between moderates and
fundamentalists in the Sikh Temple, and not to any fact or comment referenced
in Schedule A.  It is, therefore, unresponsive to the question, and is struck.

[
145
]

The defendants’ answer to the plaintiffs’ demand
for particulars in relation to the plea of fair comment, goes on to relate
certain “facts and matters relied on in support of the allegation that the words
set out above (in sub-paragraphs a to u) are true”.  These are set out in
certain further sub-paragraphs, designated by letters (a) to (u).  To the
extent that these sub-paragraphs relate to the same lettered paragraphs that
have been struck, they too are struck.  To the extent that these sub-paragraphs
relate to same lettered paragraphs that have not been struck, they are not
struck.

[
146
]

The plaintiffs have delivered the following
demand for particulars:

2.(b)     As to paragraph 7 of the Statement of
Defence:  To the extent, if any, that the words complained of “meant and were
understood to mean that the Plaintiffs had engaged in criminal conduct, namely
the misappropriation of funds from the Temple, and that therefore they were
dishonest and corrupt” as alleged in paragraph 15 of the Statement of Claim,
what facts do you rely upon as a basis for publishing those words?

[
147
]

The defendants’ answer is as follows:

2.(b)     The basis for the words listed in
Schedule “A” of the Plaintiffs’ Statement of Claim have been described in the
Answer to demand 2(a).  As for the allegation contained in paragraph 15 of the
Statement of Claim, the Defendants, CBC and Evans, are not obliged to provide
particulars of the Plaintiffs’ allegations.

[
148
]

To the extent that this demand and answer relates
to the plea of justification, the answer is unresponsive.  The plea of
justification has been struck.  Pending any amendment to plead justification,
no particulars are required.  To the extent that the demand and answer relate
to the defendants’ plea of fair comment, the reference to the “answer to demand
2(a)” is unresponsive.  In view of my finding that the plaintiffs’ plea of
defamation will not be struck pursuant to Rule 19(24), it is incumbent upon the
defendants to provide particulars in response to demand 2(a), namely, “As to
paragraph 7 of the Statement of Defence:  Which of the words complained of were
statements of fact and which were statements of comment?”  The defendants have
answered by identifying certain statements which they assert to be of fact, but
have not identified statements of comment.  Particulars must be provided
identifying the statements of comment in the words complained of in the
Statement of Claim, including the meaning ascribed to those words by the
plaintiffs, within the time provided for in para. 132 above.

[
149
]

As for the particulars set out in the answers to
demands 3 and 4, I find those to be responsive to the demands, and sufficient.
